25/glossary/RU.html:
Глоссарий

Учебный конспект

Гипоксия и дыхательная недостаточность

Гипоксия и гипоксемия

Гипоксемия означает снижение напряжения кислорода в артериальной крови (PaO₂), а тканевая гипоксия — недостаточность доступного кислорода для клеточного метаболизма. Они могут сочетаться, но не тождественны: при анемии PaO₂ может быть нормальным, хотя доставка O₂ уменьшена.

Типы тканевой гипоксии

Выделяют гипоксемическую, анемическую, циркуляторную и гистотоксическую гипоксию. Это физиологическая классификация по нарушенному звену: оксигенация крови, её кислородная ёмкость, перфузия или клеточное использование O₂.

Кислородное содержание крови

CaO₂ (мл O₂/дл) ≈ 1,34 × Hb (г/дл) × SaO₂ (доля) + 0,0031 × PaO₂ (мм рт. ст.). Большая часть O₂ связана с гемоглобином; поэтому нормальная сатурация не исключает низкого CaO₂ при анемии.

Доставка кислорода тканям

DO₂ (мл/мин) = сердечный выброс (л/мин) × CaO₂ (мл/дл) × 10. При Hb 15 г/дл, SaO₂ 0,98, PaO₂ 95 мм рт. ст. и выбросе 5 л/мин доставка около 1000 мл/мин. Это доставка, а не потребление кислорода.

Дыхательная недостаточность

Дыхательная недостаточность — неспособность дыхательной системы обеспечить адекватный газообмен. Тип I характеризуется прежде всего гипоксемией, тип II — гиперкапнией вследствие недостаточной альвеолярной вентиляции; оба нарушения могут сосуществовать. Клинические пороги зависят от контекста и высоты.

Альвеолярно-артериальный градиент

A–aDO₂ = PAO₂ − PaO₂. При чистой гиповентиляции градиент может оставаться нормальным, тогда как V/Q-несоответствие, шунт и диффузионные нарушения часто увеличивают его. Возраст, FiO₂ и барометрическое давление влияют на интерпретацию.

Гиперкапния и альвеолярная вентиляция

При постоянной продукции CO₂ PaCO₂ обратно пропорционально альвеолярной вентиляции: PaCO₂ ≈ 0,863 × V̇CO₂ / V̇A, если V̇CO₂ в мл/мин, а V̇A в л/мин. Рост мёртвого пространства повышает требуемую минутную вентиляцию для удаления CO₂.

V/Q-несоответствие

При низком V/Q кровь покидает плохо вентилируемые альвеолы с недостаточной оксигенацией; при высоком V/Q часть вентиляции малоэффективна из-за низкой перфузии. Смешивание крови из разных единиц лёгкого определяет итоговую PaO₂.

Шунт и кислородная терапия

При истинном право-левом шунте часть крови минует вентилируемые альвеолы; увеличение FiO₂ улучшает оксигенацию меньше, чем при типичном V/Q-несоответствии. Это качественное различие, не абсолютный диагностический тест.

Физиологический анализ подраздела

Терминологическая работа: дайте точные определения двум ключевым величинам и различите их единицы. Гипоксемия и тканевая гипоксия не тождественны. Доставка кислорода определяется содержанием O₂ в крови и сердечным выбросом; нарушения V/Q, шунт, гиповентиляция и диффузионные ограничения имеют разные механизмы.

После операции появилась внезапная одышка и тахикардия. Возможны V/Q-нарушения, включая лёгочную эмболию; это клиническая гипотеза, а не диагноз по газам крови. Требуется срочная очная оценка.

Этап 3. Интеграция

Гипоксемия при сниженной PaCO₂ и повышенном A–a градиенте требует анализа V/Q, шунта и диффузии с учётом анамнеза и инструментальных данных. Не используйте учебную модель для лечения пациента.

Физиологический анализ подраздела

Лабораторный протокол раздела 25: зафиксируйте исходные данные, переменную, контролируемые условия и расчёт. При Hb=8 г/дл и SaO₂=0,98 содержание O₂ может быть значительно снижено даже при нормальной SpO₂. Доставка DO₂=CO×CaO₂ требует согласования единиц и оценки сердечного выброса. Отделите наблюдение от интерпретации и укажите погрешности.

1/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Learning material

Key idea

Respiration is a linked functional system. Ventilation renews alveolar gas; diffusion transfers O₂ and CO₂ across the blood–gas barrier; perfusion brings blood to alveoli; blood carries gases; and tissues use O₂ in mitochondria. Failure at any link can limit oxygen delivery.

1. Respiration as a functional system

External respiration includes ventilation and gas exchange between alveoli and blood. O₂ is then carried mainly by haemoglobin, enters cells, and supports oxidative phosphorylation. Metabolic CO₂ follows the reverse path. Respiration, ventilation, and gas exchange are therefore not synonyms.

2. Principal functions

  • O₂ uptake and CO₂ elimination through matching ventilation to perfusion.
  • Rapid acid–base regulation through V̇A and PaCO₂.
  • Warming, humidification, filtration, and mucociliary defence.
  • Airflow for phonation, cough, and sneeze.
  • Metabolic functions of pulmonary endothelium.

3. Functional anatomy

The conducting zone extends to terminal bronchioles, conditions air, and forms anatomical dead space. The respiratory zone begins at respiratory bronchioles and includes alveolar ducts and alveoli. A thin blood–gas barrier, large area, and dense capillary network support diffusion.

Type II alveolar cells produce surfactant, which lowers surface tension. The pleura mechanically couples lungs to the chest wall. The diaphragm is the main muscle of quiet inspiration.

4. Stages of gas transfer

StageProcessLocationAssessment
VentilationRenewal of alveolar gasAirways and alveoliVT, f, V̇E, V̇A, PaCO₂
DiffusionTransfer down pressure gradientsBlood–gas barrierPaO₂, A–a, DLCO
PerfusionPulmonary capillary flowPulmonary circulationQ̇, V̇A/Q̇
TransportHb binding and dissolved gasesBloodSaO₂, Hb, CaO₂
Tissue useO₂ consumptionMitochondriaV̇O₂

5. Mechanics of the breathing cycle

During inspiration diaphragmatic contraction enlarges the thorax. Ppl becomes more negative, Ptp = Palv − Ppl rises, lungs expand, and a brief fall of Palv below atmospheric pressure drives inward flow. At end inspiration Palv again equals atmospheric pressure. Quiet expiration is usually passive: elastic recoil reduces volume, Palv becomes slightly positive, and air leaves.

6. Minute and alveolar ventilation

VariableFormula / meaningResting guideInterpretation
VTVolume of one breath≈ 500 mLDepends on body size
fBreathing frequency≈ 12–16/minDoes not define ventilation without VT
V̇EVT × f≈ 6–8 L/minIncludes dead space
VDVolume without gas exchange≈ 150 mLPhysiological VD may be larger
V̇A(VT − VD) × f≈ 4–5 L/minDetermines CO₂ removal, other factors equal

Common student error

Equal V̇E does not mean equal V̇A. 500 mL × 12/min gives V̇E 6 L/min and V̇A 4.2 L/min at VD 150 mL; 250 mL × 24/min gives the same V̇E but only 2.4 L/min V̇A.

7. Ventilation, CO₂, and acid–base status

At stable CO₂ production, PaCO₂ is inversely proportional to V̇A. Hypoventilation retains CO₂ and favours respiratory acidosis; hyperventilation removes excess CO₂ and favours respiratory alkalosis. The relevant variable is effective alveolar ventilation, not merely chest movement.

8. Clinical significance

Normal chest excursion does not guarantee normal oxygenation or O₂ delivery. Oxygenation depends on alveolar PO₂, diffusion, and V̇A/Q̇; O₂ content mainly on Hb and saturation; delivery also on cardiac output. SpO₂ does not measure PaCO₂ and cannot exclude hypoventilation or anaemia.

Academic foundation

Respiration integrates ventilation, alveolar diffusion, pulmonary perfusion, blood gas transport and tissue oxygen consumption. Failure of any link can reduce oxygen delivery despite preserved measurements elsewhere. Partial pressure, saturation and oxygen content are distinct quantities.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Section-specific academic study

External respiration integrates bulk airflow, regional ventilation, diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier and pulmonary perfusion. Gas exchange depends on partial-pressure gradients, membrane properties and ventilation–perfusion matching. Most O₂ is carried by hemoglobin; PaO₂ describes dissolved O₂ tension rather than total oxygen content.

Conceptual checkpoint

Normal SpO₂ does not rule out hypoventilation: CO₂ clearance requires PaCO₂ or other appropriate measures.

Worked physiological example

With unchanged ventilation, oxygen delivery may fall in anemia: blood O₂ content depends chiefly on hemoglobin, not PaO₂ alone.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Learning material

1/practice/EN.html:
Practice

Learning material
Which stage transfers O₂ across the blood–gas barrier?

This is diffusion down a partial-pressure gradient.

Which statement about VD is correct?

VD reduces the effective fraction of each VT.

VT 500 mL × f 12/min: V̇E (L/min)?

V̇E = 0.5 × 12 = 6 L/min.

VT 500 mL, VD 150 mL, f 12/min: V̇A (L/min)?

V̇A = (0.50 − 0.15) × 12 = 4.2 L/min.

VT 250 mL, VD 150 mL, f 24/min: V̇A (L/min)?

V̇A = (0.25 − 0.15) × 24 = 2.4 L/min.

Find the error: “lungs pull air in themselves.”

Respiratory muscles create the pressure gradient; lungs follow the chest wall through pleural coupling.

After sedation f and VT fall. What is expected?

Reduced V̇A retains CO₂.

Complete: diaphragm → Ppl → Ptp → volume → flow.

Diaphragm contraction → more negative Ppl → higher Ptp → lung expansion → Palv below atmosphere → inspiration.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

An adult at rest has VT=500 mL and a rate of 12/min. Assume physiological dead space of 150 mL. Calculate alveolar ventilation, compare it with minute ventilation, and explain the difference.

Worked solution

V̇A=(500−150)×12/1000=4.20 L/min. V̇E=500×12/1000=6.00 L/min; dead-space ventilation is 1.80 L/min. Converting mL to L keeps the units consistent.

Meaning and model limitations

V̇E describes all moved gas, whereas V̇A describes renewal of gas-exchanging regions. Equal minute ventilation does not ensure equal CO₂ clearance. The calculation assumes fixed VD and omits regional heterogeneity.

2/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Conducting and respiratory zones

The conducting zone comprises the nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and terminal bronchioles. It transports, warms, humidifies and filters inspired air; meaningful gas exchange does not occur there. The respiratory zone begins at respiratory bronchioles and includes alveolar ducts and sacs, where O₂ and CO₂ exchange with blood.

Branching and resistance

As airways branch, each lumen becomes smaller but the aggregate cross-sectional area of numerous peripheral airways increases greatly. Flow velocity therefore falls near alveoli. In healthy lungs, medium-sized bronchi contribute substantially to total resistance, rather than the smallest bronchioles. Poiseuille’s law applies to laminar flow in an ideal rigid tube, not to all features of real airways.

Alveolar–capillary barrier

The diffusion path includes a fluid/surfactant layer, type I alveolar epithelium, a thin interstitium or fused basement membranes, and capillary endothelium. Type II pneumocytes produce surfactant and support epithelial repair. Transfer depends on surface area, barrier thickness, diffusion properties and the partial-pressure gradient (Fick’s principle).

Mucociliary defense

Ciliated epithelium and mucus trap particles and move them toward the pharynx. Cough assists clearance from larger airways. Alveolar macrophages remove particles in distal regions lacking cilia. Impaired clearance increases secretion retention and infection risk.

Animated schematic: scale and branch counts are illustrative.

Academic foundation

The conducting zone transports, warms, humidifies and filters air; gas exchange occurs mainly in alveoli. Type I pneumocytes form a thin diffusion interface, while type II cells produce surfactant and support epithelial repair. Capillary endothelium and interstitium also affect gas transfer.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Academic extension: Conducting versus respiratory zones

The conducting zone through terminal bronchioles warms, humidifies and filters air but contributes negligible gas exchange. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli constitute the exchange zone. Type I pneumocytes form a thin exchange surface; type II cells produce surfactant and participate in epithelial repair. Alveolar macrophages provide cellular defense. Barrier thickness and area influence diffusion alongside gas properties.

Conceptual checkpoint

Anatomical dead space is not identical to physiological dead space, which also includes alveolar dead space.

Worked physiological example

Conducting airways do not directly exchange alveolar gases; their volume contributes to anatomical dead space.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Teaching draft

Five key connections

Clinical bridge

Teaching draft

Clinical physiology

In a patient with interstitial fibrosis the alveolar–capillary barrier thickens. During exercise, red-cell transit time through pulmonary capillaries shortens. Explain why oxygenation may become impaired during exercise before it does at rest.

Physiological explanation

A thicker barrier reduces diffusing conductance. Shorter contact time may prevent capillary PO₂ from equilibrating with alveolar PO₂. Actual oxygenation also depends on V/Q, ventilation and hemoglobin.

Academic analysis

Alveolar-capillary barrier and alveolar cells

Type I pneumocytes cover most gas-exchange surface; type II pneumocytes produce and recycle surfactant and replenish alveolar epithelium. The gas-exchange barrier comprises alveolar epithelium, basement membranes, a thin interstitium and capillary endothelium. Greater thickness or smaller surface area lowers diffusing conductance and may reduce DLCO.

Quantitative and analytical task

With constant area and pressure gradient, barrier thickness doubles. Predict diffusion flux using the simplified Fick model and state one limitation.

Reveal worked answer

Flux approximately halves (V̇gas ∝ A·ΔP/T). Real lungs may also change capillary recruitment, perfusion and V/Q distribution.

2/practice/EN.html:
Practice

Teaching draft

Worked reasoning task

At a constant volume flow of 6 L/min, aggregate cross-sectional area rises 50-fold. What happens to mean linear velocity? It falls 50-fold because Q = vA.

Animated schematic: scale and branch counts are illustrative.

Academic extension: Conducting versus respiratory zones

The conducting zone through terminal bronchioles warms, humidifies and filters air but contributes negligible gas exchange. Respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveoli constitute the exchange zone. Type I pneumocytes form a thin exchange surface; type II cells produce surfactant and participate in epithelial repair. Alveolar macrophages provide cellular defense. Barrier thickness and area influence diffusion alongside gas properties.

Investigation task

Why may interstitial thickening impair O₂ transfer more during exercise than at rest? Distinguish the structural and hemodynamic factors.

Solution and interpretation

Fick’s law predicts lower flux with greater barrier thickness. Exercise shortens pulmonary capillary red-cell transit time, potentially exposing limited diffusion reserve. V/Q matching and capillary recruitment also matter.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

Air flows through a conducting-airway model at 6 L/min. The aggregate area of parallel channels is 2 cm². Find mean linear velocity in m/s, then increase aggregate area to 20 cm² at unchanged volume flow.

Worked solution

6 L/min=100 cm³/s. From Q=vA, v=100/2=50 cm/s=0.50 m/s. At 20 cm², velocity is 5 cm/s=0.05 m/s, a tenfold reduction.

Meaning and model limitations

Volume flow and linear velocity are distinct. Large aggregate distal airway area slows convective movement. This geometric model does not determine molecular diffusion across the alveolar barrier.

3/objectives/EN.html:
Learning objectives

Teaching draft

Learning outcomes

After the lesson, learners should distinguish alveolar, pleural and transpulmonary pressures; explain inspiration and expiration; calculate compliance and resistance; and connect mechanics to work of breathing.

Pressure gradients

Air flows because of a pressure difference between the atmosphere and alveoli. During quiet inspiration, diaphragm contraction enlarges the thoracic cavity, alveolar pressure becomes slightly subatmospheric and air enters. At end-inspiration, with no flow, alveolar pressure returns approximately to atmospheric pressure. Passive expiration reverses the gradient through elastic recoil.

Transpulmonary pressure

Transpulmonary pressure Pᴸ = Palv − Ppl is the distending pressure across the lung. Pleural pressure is usually negative relative to atmosphere during quiet breathing, but values depend on posture, respiratory phase and measurement method. Increasing transpulmonary pressure expands the lung; volume follows a nonlinear pressure–volume relation.

Compliance and hysteresis

Static compliance C = ΔV/ΔP is the change in lung volume per change in distending pressure under no-flow conditions. It depends on tissue elasticity and surface tension. Inflation and deflation pressure–volume curves differ (hysteresis), partly because of surfactant behavior and alveolar recruitment. A linear compliance approximation applies only over a limited volume range.

Resistance and work of breathing

For simplified steady laminar flow, resistance R = ΔP/flow. Real airways branch and flow may be transitional or turbulent, so resistance is not necessarily constant. Work of breathing includes elastic work (distending lungs and chest wall) and resistive work (overcoming flow resistance). Obstruction tends to increase resistive work; reduced compliance increases elastic work.

Subsection physiology analysis

Outcome: define the mechanism, explain its causal chain and state model limits. Diaphragm contraction expands the thorax and makes pleural pressure more negative. Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus pleural pressure and contributes to lung distension.

Teaching draft

Assessment questions

1. At the end of quiet inspiration with zero airflow, alveolar pressure relative to atmospheric pressure is:

With open airways and no flow, the alveolar–atmospheric driving gradient is absent.

2. Palv = 0 cm H₂O and Ppl = −6 cm H₂O. What is transpulmonary pressure?

Pᴸ = Palv − Ppl = 0 − (−6) = +6 cm H₂O.

By C = ΔV/ΔP, greater compliance means a greater volume change at the same pressure increment within the modeled range.

4. Which change most directly increases resistive work of breathing?

Maintaining the same flow against higher resistance requires a larger driving pressure and greater resistive work.

5. Why do lung inflation and deflation curves differ?

Hysteresis reflects volume history, surfactant-dependent surface tension and alveolar recruitment.

3/clinical/EN.html:
Clinical bridge

Teaching draft

Clinical reasoning

A patient with airflow obstruction exhales more slowly than usual. Explain why higher resistance increases the pressure gradient needed to maintain flow, and why dynamic airway compression may occur during forced expiration. Do not infer a diagnosis from this vignette alone.

Explanation

For the same flow, increased R requires a larger ΔP. During forced expiration pleural pressure may become positive; beyond the equal-pressure point, some intrathoracic airways narrow and limit flow.

Advanced academic physiology

Equation of motion of the respiratory system

Neglecting inertial forces, respiratory muscle pressure balances elastic recoil and flow resistance. In a simplified model ΔP = E·ΔV + R·V̇, where E is elastance (inverse compliance), R is resistance, and V̇ is flow. The elastic term depends on volume; the resistive term depends on flow. During forced breathing resistance is nonlinear, limiting this approximation.

Calculation and analysis

Given compliance 0.20 L/cm H₂O, ΔV = 0.50 L, R = 2 cm H₂O·s/L and flow 0.50 L/s, calculate the required pressure difference.

Show solution and physiological explanation

Elastic pressure = 0.50/0.20 = 2.5 cm H₂O; resistive pressure = 1.0 cm H₂O; total = 3.5 cm H₂O.

Educational model. References: Guyton & Hall; West; Boron & Boulpaep.

Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar minus pleural pressure, not merely airway pressure.

Teaching draft

Advanced academic physiology

Equation of motion of the respiratory system

Neglecting inertial forces, respiratory muscle pressure balances elastic recoil and flow resistance. In a simplified model ΔP = E·ΔV + R·V̇, where E is elastance (inverse compliance), R is resistance, and V̇ is flow. The elastic term depends on volume; the resistive term depends on flow. During forced breathing resistance is nonlinear, limiting this approximation.

Calculation and analysis

Show solution and physiological explanation

Elastic pressure = 0.50/0.20 = 2.5 cm H₂O; resistive pressure = 1.0 cm H₂O; total = 3.5 cm H₂O.

Discussion with explanation

Why do lung and chest wall recoil in opposite directions when the pleural space opens?

Show explanation

Near functional residual capacity, lung recoil is inward and chest-wall recoil is outward. Mechanical coupling through the pleural space maintains their shared equilibrium.

4/objectives/EN.html:
Learning objectives

Teaching draft

Learning outcomes

  1. Explain muscle contraction → Ppl change → Palv change → flow.
  2. Calculate Ptp, τ and resistive pressure drop.
  3. Distinguish quiet and forced expiration.

What drives airflow

Airflow follows the pressure gradient between atmosphere and alveoli. At the start of quiet inspiration, diaphragm contraction expands the thorax; pleural pressure becomes more negative, alveoli expand, and alveolar pressure briefly falls below atmospheric pressure. Air enters until the pressures equalize.

Phases of quiet breathing

At end-expiration flow is zero, alveolar pressure is approximately atmospheric, and pleural pressure remains negative. During inspiration alveolar pressure commonly falls by roughly 1 cm H₂O and returns to atmospheric at end-inspiration. During passive expiration elastic recoil creates a small positive alveolar pressure gradient. Values are illustrative and depend on conditions.

Transpulmonary pressure

Transpulmonary pressure Ptp = Palv − Ppl is the distending pressure across the lung. With Palv = 0 and Ppl = −5 cm H₂O, Ptp is +5 cm H₂O. More negative pleural pressure during inspiration generally increases Ptp and lung volume. Ptp is not the airflow-driving gradient (Patm − Palv).

Diaphragm and intercostal muscles

The diaphragm is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration. Its contraction lowers the dome and enlarges the vertical thoracic dimension; external intercostals assist rib elevation. Quiet expiration is usually passive through elastic recoil; forced expiration recruits abdominal muscles and internal intercostals.

Resistance and time constant

For a simplified resistive segment ΔP = R × V̇. In a linear single-compartment model τ = R × C sets the characteristic filling and emptying time. About 63% of a step response occurs after one τ and about 95% after three. Real lungs are heterogeneous and both resistance and compliance are nonlinear.

Work of breathing and model limits

Mechanical inspiratory work is the integral ∫P dV and includes elastic and resistive loads. Higher resistance requires a larger pressure drop for the same flow; lower compliance requires more distending pressure for the same volume change. In vivo, pleural pressure, muscle effort, regional heterogeneity and airflow interact dynamically.

Subsection physiology analysis

Outcome: define the mechanism, explain its causal chain and state model limits. During quiet inspiration alveolar pressure transiently falls below atmospheric pressure; passive expiration follows elastic recoil. Airflow depends on the pressure gradient and airway resistance.

Teaching draft

Quantitative case

At flow 0.4 L/s and R = 3 cm H₂O·s/L, calculate the resistive pressure drop. At C = 0.15 L/cm H₂O, find the quasi-static distending pressure change needed for a 0.45 L volume rise.

Laboratory: respiratory cycle

Single-compartment model: volume follows a cosine waveform, flow is its derivative, and Palv = −R·flow for inward-positive flow. Ppl is estimated from Ptp = 5 + ΔV/C. Educational only; not a clinical diagnostic model.

Task and interpretation

1. Double resistance and compare Palv amplitude at fixed volume and rate. 2. Lower compliance and compare Ppl amplitude. 3. Explain why Palv approaches zero at zero flow.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

In a passive one-compartment model, R=3 cm H₂O·s/L and C=0.20 L/cm H₂O. Find time constant τ. What fraction of the initial excess volume remains after three time constants?

Worked solution

τ=RC=3×0.20=0.60 s. With ΔV(t)=ΔV₀e^(−t/τ), after 3τ=1.80 s the remaining fraction is e⁻³≈0.050, or 5%; about 95% of excess volume has emptied.

Meaning and model limitations

Higher R or C slows passive emptying. An overly short expiration can favor gas trapping. The model omits active muscles, dynamic compression and regional differences in time constants.

5/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Pressures: choosing a reference

In respiratory mechanics atmospheric pressure is often set to 0 cm H₂O (gauge pressure). Alveolar Palv and pleural Ppl are then expressed relative to atmosphere. These are not absolute pressures: sea-level atmospheric pressure is about 760 mmHg.

Transpulmonary pressure

Transpulmonary pressure Ptp = Palv − Ppl describes the lung-distending pressure. At end quiet expiration Palv ≈ 0 and Ppl ≈ −5 cm H₂O, giving Ptp ≈ +5 cm H₂O. Negative pleural pressure does not mean alveolar gas pressure is always negative.

Inspiration and expiration: flow gradient

At the onset of inspiration diaphragm contraction makes Ppl more negative, raising Ptp and lung volume. Palv briefly falls to about −1 cm H₂O, drawing air in. At end inspiration Palv returns near 0. During passive expiration Palv briefly becomes positive, driving air out, and returns near 0 at end expiration.

Pressure and volume: compliance

For quasi-static changes compliance C = ΔV/ΔPtp. If ΔV = 0.40 L for ΔPtp = 2 cm H₂O, C = 0.20 L/cm H₂O. This is an average over the specified part of the pressure-volume curve, not a universal constant: the relationship is nonlinear and exhibits hysteresis.

Pneumothorax and loss of distending gradient

When the pleural space communicates with the atmosphere, Ppl on that side may approach atmospheric pressure. If Palv is also near 0, Ptp falls and lung recoil promotes collapse. The extent depends on the leak and clinical conditions; tension pneumothorax is an emergency.

Surfactant and Laplace’s law

Pulmonary surfactant is produced mainly by type II alveolar cells. Its phospholipids and proteins lower surface tension, particularly as alveolar surface area decreases, promoting stability and reducing work of breathing. The simplified spherical-bubble relation P = 2T/r illustrates tension T and radius r but does not fully represent interconnected alveoli in a living lung.

Elastic recoil and hysteresis

Elastic recoil reflects tissue elastin and collagen as well as surface tension at the air–liquid interface. Inflation and deflation pressure–volume curves differ (hysteresis), partly owing to surfactant behavior and recruitment. A constant compliance is therefore only a local approximation.

Measurement and interpretation limits

Pleural pressure is often estimated indirectly using esophageal pressure. This approximation requires proper balloon positioning and interpretation; regional gradients, body position and respiratory muscle activity affect the result. The simulator below represents one simplified state, not a complete breathing cycle.

Academic foundation

Compliance is volume change per change in transpulmonary pressure. Surfactant lowers surface tension, supports alveolar stability and reduces inspiratory work. Laplace's law illustrates an ideal spherical interface, but real alveoli are mechanically interconnected.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Physiological mechanism

Surfactant is synthesized by type II alveolar epithelial cells. Its phospholipids and SP-B/SP-C reduce surface tension, particularly as surface area decreases. ΔP=2T/r describes an ideal spherical interface, not the full interconnected alveolar network.

Practice

Teaching draft

Calculation problem

At end expiration Palv = 0 and Ppl = −5 cm H₂O. During a breath hold with open airways Ppl = −8 and Palv = 0. With average C = 0.20 L/cm H₂O, estimate ΔV.

Solution

Laboratory: pressure and distension

Change Palv and Ppl. Calculate Ptp and the expected volume change at selected compliance. Reference Ptp = 5 cm H₂O. This is a linear teaching model.

Caution: ΔV = C × (Ptp − 5) is a linear illustration, not a patient-specific prediction.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

In a quasi-static experiment volume rises 0.45 L for a transpulmonary pressure increase of 3 cm H₂O. Find compliance. A repeat requires 6 cm H₂O for the same volume increase; compare the mechanical properties.

Worked solution

C=ΔV/ΔP=0.45/3=0.15 L/cm H₂O. Repeat C=0.45/6=0.075 L/cm H₂O, half the initial value. Elastance E=1/C rises from 6.67 to 13.33 cm H₂O/L.

Meaning and model limitations

Reduced compliance requires greater pressure for the same ΔV. Surfactant deficiency can increase surface loading, but C alone does not establish the cause; volume range and experimental conditions matter.

6/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Physiological mechanism 1

Airway resistance is the pressure difference between two points divided by volumetric airflow: Raw = ΔP/V̇, commonly expressed in cm H₂O·s/L. For a fixed pressure difference, higher resistance lowers flow. Actual airway resistance depends on lung volume, airway geometry, gas viscosity, flow pattern and dynamic compression during forced expiration.

Physiological mechanism 2

For steady laminar flow through a long rigid cylindrical tube, Poiseuille’s idealized law gives R = 8ηL/(πr⁴). Halving radius increases predicted resistance sixteenfold. Branching compliant airways and transitional or turbulent flow mean this law must not be applied uncritically to the whole bronchial tree.

Physiological mechanism 3

Small bronchioles are numerous and arranged in parallel, with a large combined cross-sectional area. Thus upper and medium-sized airways usually contribute more to total resistance during normal breathing than a single terminal bronchiole. Small-airway disease can nevertheless substantially limit flow.

Physiological mechanism 4

Work of breathing is W = ∫P dV. Elastic work stretches lung and chest wall; resistive work is dissipated by airflow and tissue deformation. The area of a pressure–volume loop reflects energy lost per cycle. Obstruction raises resistive loading, whereas reduced compliance raises elastic loading.

Practice

Teaching draft

Physiological mechanism

Problem 1: ΔP = 3 cm H₂O, V̇ = 0.5 L/s. Raw = 6 cm H₂O·s/L. Problem 2: the radius of an ideal tube falls by 20%; Rnew/Rold = 1/(0.8⁴) ≈ 2.44. Do not extrapolate this factor directly to the entire airway tree.

Academic analysis: Airway resistance: radius and flow regime

For laminar flow in a rigid cylindrical tube, R=8ηL/(πr⁴). Halving radius therefore raises theoretical resistance 16-fold if other variables remain constant. Real airways are compliant and branching, flow can become transitional or turbulent, and peripheral airways act in parallel. During forced expiration, intrathoracic pressure can dynamically compress airways.

Exercise

If an ideal tube radius falls to 80% of baseline, calculate Rnew/Rbaseline and state two limits of applying this to lungs.

Solution

Rnew/Rbaseline=1/(0.8⁴)=2.44. Real airways are not rigid cylinders; flow regime and parallel branching alter the relationship.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

An ideal rigid tube narrows from radius 2 to 1 mm. Viscosity and length stay fixed and flow is laminar. By what factor does resistance rise? Then explain the change in flow at unchanged driving pressure.

Worked solution

R₂/R₁=(r₁/r₂)⁴=(2/1)⁴=16. From Q=ΔP/R, Q₂/Q₁=1/16. Preserving baseline Q in this model requires a sixteenfold pressure increase.

Meaning and model limitations

Radius strongly affects a single channel’s resistance. Bronchi form a branching network and high-speed flow need not remain laminar. A factor of 16 is therefore not a quantitative prediction of a patient’s bronchospasm severity.

7/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

1. Lung volumes and capacities

Tidal volume (VT) is the volume moved in a quiet breath, often about 0.5 L in a resting adult, with substantial individual variation. Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV) is the additional volume inhaled after a normal inspiration; expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is exhaled after normal expiration. Residual volume (RV) remains after maximal expiration.

2. Lung volumes and capacities

Vital capacity VC = IRV + VT + ERV. Total lung capacity TLC = VC + RV. Functional residual capacity FRC = ERV + RV, and inspiratory capacity IC = VT + IRV. These capacities are sums of component volumes, not independent compartments.

3. Lung volumes and capacities

Simple spirometry measures volume passing the mouth but cannot directly measure RV, FRC or TLC, because residual gas is not exhaled. Absolute volumes require body plethysmography or gas dilution/washout methods. In obstruction, gas dilution may underestimate poorly ventilated regions.

4. Lung volumes and capacities

Forced vital capacity (FVC) and forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV₁) depend on effort and maneuver quality. FEV₁/FVC helps assess airflow limitation; diagnosis should not rely on a single arbitrary fixed cutoff without considering age, reference values and test quality.

5. Lung volumes and capacities

Minute ventilation V̇E = VT × f; alveolar ventilation V̇A = (VT − VD) × f, where VD is dead-space volume and f is breathing frequency. Rapid shallow breathing can reduce alveolar ventilation despite unchanged minute ventilation. This teaching model holds VD constant, unlike some disease states.

8/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

1. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Minute ventilation VE is the total volume entering or leaving the airways per minute: VE = VT × f. It is not the amount of fresh air reaching gas-exchanging alveoli because part of each breath occupies conducting airways. With VT = 500 mL and f = 12/min, VE = 6 L/min.

2. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Anatomical dead space VD,anat comprises conducting airways without appreciable gas exchange. In a resting adult it is often approximately 150 mL but varies with body size, posture and lung volume. Physiological dead space includes anatomical and alveolar dead space (ventilated alveoli with insufficient perfusion).

3. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Alveolar ventilation VA = (VT − VD) × f for a fixed dead-space volume and regular breaths. With VT = 500 mL, VD = 150 mL and f = 12/min, VA = 4.2 L/min. With VT = 300 mL and f = 20/min, minute ventilation remains 6 L/min but VA is only 3 L/min. Thus rapid shallow breathing is less efficient for alveolar gas renewal.

4. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

At steady state with constant CO₂ production, PaCO₂ is inversely related to effective alveolar ventilation: PaCO₂ ≈ 0.863 × VCO₂ / VA, when VCO₂ is in mL/min, VA in L/min and pressure in mmHg. For VCO₂ = 200 mL/min and VA = 4.32 L/min, PaCO₂ is approximately 40 mmHg. The equation is not a precise prediction during transients or marked V/Q inequality.

5. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

The Bohr equation estimates physiological dead space from mixed expired PĒCO₂ and alveolar PACO₂: VD/VT = (PACO₂ − PĒCO₂)/PACO₂. The clinical Enghoff modification substitutes arterial PaCO₂ for PACO₂ and therefore also captures effects of shunt and V/Q inequality; the two measures are not interchangeable.

Change VT, f and VD. Compare minute and alveolar ventilation; the graph shows the fraction of each breath reaching the gas-exchange region.

Simplified model: VD is fixed per breath; leaks and V/Q inequality are ignored. If VT ≤ VD, VA is set to zero.

Academic foundation

Minute ventilation differs from alveolar ventilation because part of each breath ventilates dead space. At constant CO₂ production, PaCO₂ is inversely related to alveolar ventilation in a steady-state approximation. Rapid shallow breathing may preserve minute ventilation while reducing effective alveolar ventilation.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Mechanism

Minute ventilation V̇E=VT·f includes conducting-airway gas. Alveolar ventilation V̇A=(VT−VD)·f estimates fresh gas reaching exchange units. At constant CO₂ production, steady-state PaCO₂ varies inversely with V̇A. Physiological dead space is not a fixed universal volume.

Physiological mechanism

Alveolar ventilation is the volume of fresh gas reaching gas-exchanging lung units each minute. At constant physiological dead space, V̇A = (VT − VD) × f. With VT 500 mL, VD 150 mL and f 12/min, V̇A is 4.2 L/min. Reducing VT to 250 mL while doubling f to 24/min maintains minute ventilation at 6 L/min but lowers alveolar ventilation to 2.4 L/min. Equal minute ventilation does not imply equal CO₂ clearance.

Reference reading: West, Respiratory Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology; ERS/ATS (spirometry).

Conceptual checkpoint

Equal minute ventilation does not imply equal alveolar ventilation, especially when tidal volume changes.

Worked physiological example

For tidal volume 500 mL, dead space 150 mL and rate 12/min, alveolar ventilation is (500−150)×12 = 4200 mL/min.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Derive VA. Explain why equal VE does not guarantee equal CO₂ elimination. Discuss assumptions of the alveolar ventilation equation.

1. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Minute ventilation VE is the total volume entering or leaving the airways per minute: VE = VT × f. It is not the amount of fresh air reaching gas-exchanging alveoli because part of each breath occupies conducting airways. With VT = 500 mL and f = 12/min, VE = 6 L/min.

2. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Anatomical dead space VD,anat comprises conducting airways without appreciable gas exchange. In a resting adult it is often approximately 150 mL but varies with body size, posture and lung volume. Physiological dead space includes anatomical and alveolar dead space (ventilated alveoli with insufficient perfusion).

3. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

Alveolar ventilation VA = (VT − VD) × f for a fixed dead-space volume and regular breaths. With VT = 500 mL, VD = 150 mL and f = 12/min, VA = 4.2 L/min. With VT = 300 mL and f = 20/min, minute ventilation remains 6 L/min but VA is only 3 L/min. Thus rapid shallow breathing is less efficient for alveolar gas renewal.

4. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

At steady state with constant CO₂ production, PaCO₂ is inversely related to effective alveolar ventilation: PaCO₂ ≈ 0.863 × VCO₂ / VA, when VCO₂ is in mL/min, VA in L/min and pressure in mmHg. For VCO₂ = 200 mL/min and VA = 4.32 L/min, PaCO₂ is approximately 40 mmHg. The equation is not a precise prediction during transients or marked V/Q inequality.

5. Alveolar ventilation and dead space

The Bohr equation estimates physiological dead space from mixed expired PĒCO₂ and alveolar PACO₂: VD/VT = (PACO₂ − PĒCO₂)/PACO₂. The clinical Enghoff modification substitutes arterial PaCO₂ for PACO₂ and therefore also captures effects of shunt and V/Q inequality; the two measures are not interchangeable.

Subsection physiology analysis

Oral explanation: trace stimulus to response without mistaking correlation for causation. Minute ventilation is VT×f; alveolar ventilation is (VT−VD)×f. At constant CO₂ production, PaCO₂ varies approximately inversely with alveolar ventilation.

9/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

1. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

Diffusion is passive gas movement down a partial-pressure gradient. Alveolar PO₂ is often near 100 mmHg, while mixed venous blood entering pulmonary capillaries has PO₂ near 40 mmHg. Values vary with altitude, ventilation and metabolism.

2. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

Fick’s law in simplified form: gas flux ∝ (A/T) × D × ΔP. A is available area, T barrier thickness, D diffusion coefficient and ΔP partial-pressure difference. Doubling thickness halves predicted flux when other factors are fixed.

3. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

The alveolar-capillary barrier consists of alveolar epithelium, a thin interstitium with fused basement membranes in its thinnest regions, and capillary endothelium. Oxygen dissolves in lining fluid, crosses membranes and binds to erythrocyte hemoglobin.

4. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

At sea level while breathing room air, O₂ transfer is usually perfusion-limited: capillary blood approaches alveolar PO₂ before transit ends. Thickened membranes, exercise and hypoxia can make diffusion limitation more important.

5. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

CO₂ is more soluble than O₂ and diffuses more readily under comparable conditions. Nevertheless, ventilation and perfusion disturbances can cause hypercapnia. Partial-pressure differences alone do not quantify transferred gas without solubility and binding.

6. Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

DLCO measures diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide using a very low test concentration. It depends on membrane conductance, pulmonary capillary blood volume and CO binding to hemoglobin; interpretation accounts for hemoglobin and test method.

Academic foundation

Fick's law predicts faster diffusion with larger area and partial-pressure gradient and slower diffusion with a thicker barrier. Solubility and molecular properties also matter. This physical model explains directions of change but does not replace clinical measurement of lung diffusing capacity.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Mechanism and physiological significance

O₂ transfer depends on partial-pressure gradient, alveolar-capillary surface area, barrier thickness and diffusion coefficient: gas flux ∝ A·D·ΔP/T. Thickening reduces flux if other conditions are fixed. At rest, capillary O₂ normally equilibrates before transit ends; exercise and interstitial disease reduce this reserve. DLCO reflects both membrane conductance and capillary blood volume and is influenced by haemoglobin.

Conceptual checkpoint

Fick’s law predicts idealized flux; measured DLCO also depends on hemoglobin and pulmonary capillary blood volume.

Worked physiological example

By Fick's law, diffusion increases with surface area and partial-pressure gradient and decreases as barrier thickness rises.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Practice

Teaching draft

Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

Gas diffusion across the alveolar-capillary barrier

Problem: area decreases to 70%, thickness rises to 140%, ΔPO₂ unchanged. Relative flux = 0.70/1.40 = 0.50 of baseline. State model limitations.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

In a controlled model diffusion area falls to 75% of baseline, barrier thickness doubles, and the partial-pressure gradient rises from 40 to 53.333 mmHg. Find relative gas transfer at fixed diffusivity.

Worked solution

J₂/J₁=(A₂/A₁)(ΔP₂/ΔP₁)/(T₂/T₁)=0.75×(53.333/40)/2≈0.50. The greater gradient does not fully offset reduced area and increased thickness.

Meaning and model limitations

Fick’s law describes transfer rate under specified conditions, not PaO₂ directly. Predicting blood oxygenation also needs perfusion, hemoglobin and transit time; O₂ and CO₂ have different diffusivities.

10/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Gas composition and partial pressures

1. Composition of dry atmospheric air

Dry air contains approximately 20.95% O₂, 78.08% N₂, 0.93% argon and 0.04% CO₂ (CO₂ varies). Respiratory calculations often group nitrogen and argon as inert gases. These percentages describe dry air: humidification in the airways reduces the pressure available to other gases.

2. Dalton’s law

The total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of component partial pressures: Ptotal = ΣPi. For an ideal mixture Pi = Fi × Ptotal. At 760 mmHg, dry-air PO₂ ≈ 0.2095 × 760 = 159 mmHg. Partial pressure is not the same as blood oxygen content or hemoglobin saturation.

3. Airway humidification

At 37 °C, tracheal gas is nearly saturated with water vapor: PH₂O ≈ 47 mmHg. Therefore PIO₂ = FIO₂ × (PB − PH₂O). At sea level with FIO₂ = 0.21 and PB = 760, PIO₂ ≈ 150 mmHg. This is not alveolar PO₂: oxygen is continuously taken up by blood while CO₂ enters alveoli.

4. Alveolar gas equation

Clinical approximation: PAO₂ ≈ FIO₂(PB − 47) − PaCO₂/R, where R is the respiratory exchange ratio (often near 0.8 on a mixed diet). At 760 mmHg, FIO₂ 0.21 and PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, PAO₂ ≈ 100 mmHg. This steady-state approximation omits a small correction that can matter at high FIO₂.

5. Why alveolar gas differs from ambient air

Alveolar gas mixes with the substantial gas volume remaining in the lungs, so its composition changes more slowly than inspired gas. Oxygen diffuses into capillary blood and CO₂ into alveoli. Humidification and ongoing exchange explain typical PAO₂ near 100 and PACO₂ near 40 mmHg on room air at sea level.

6. Arterial and venous gases

For a healthy resting adult at sea level, PaO₂ is often around 80–100 mmHg, PaCO₂ 35–45 mmHg and pH 7.35–7.45. Mixed venous blood is roughly PvO₂ 40 and PvCO₂ 46 mmHg. Reference intervals depend on age, altitude, laboratory and clinical setting. PaO₂ is not oxygen content: most blood O₂ is hemoglobin-bound.

7. Alveolar–arterial oxygen difference

A–a O₂ difference = PAO₂ − PaO₂. In healthy younger adults breathing room air at sea level it is usually small, often about 5–15 mmHg, and rises with age. A larger gradient suggests V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion limitation but does not identify the cause by itself. In isolated hypoventilation, the A–a difference is usually near normal.

8. Altitude and barometric pressure

At altitude, the dry-air O₂ fraction is nearly unchanged, but barometric pressure PB and thus PIO₂ fall. Hyperventilation lowers PaCO₂ and partly restores PAO₂ relative to the uncompensated state. Acclimatization includes renal compensation of respiratory alkalosis and changes in ventilation and erythropoiesis. Altitude in meters is not a substitute for measured PB.

9. Alveolar CO₂ and ventilation

At steady state PaCO₂ is approximately inversely related to alveolar ventilation if CO₂ production is fixed: PaCO₂ ≈ 863 × V̇CO₂/V̇A (both flows in mL/min, with matching units). Doubling alveolar ventilation roughly halves PaCO₂ at fixed CO₂ production. V/Q inequality complicates interpretation.

10. Respiratory exchange ratio R

R = V̇CO₂/V̇O₂. Under steady-state mixed-diet conditions R ≈ 0.8 is commonly used; carbohydrate oxidation approaches 1.0 and fat oxidation about 0.7. In non-steady states, mouth-measured gas exchange need not equal the cellular respiratory quotient. R affects calculated PAO₂.

11. Units and common pitfalls

1 kPa ≈ 7.50 mmHg; 1 mmHg ≈ 0.133 kPa. Convert FIO₂ from percent to fraction: 21% = 0.21. Distinguish PAO₂ (alveolar), PaO₂ (arterial) and PIO₂ (humidified inspired). Using PaCO₂ to estimate alveolar CO₂ assumes PACO₂ ≈ PaCO₂.

12. Clinical use of gas equations

In hypoxemia, first establish FIO₂, PB and PaCO₂, then estimate PAO₂ and the A–a difference. Low PAO₂ can follow low PB, low FIO₂ or hypoventilation. If PAO₂ is relatively preserved but PaO₂ much lower, consider V/Q inequality, shunt or diffusion limitation. Gas equations support rather than replace clinical assessment.

Academic foundation

Humidification reduces pressure available to dry gases: PIO₂ = FiO₂ × (PB − PH₂O). The alveolar gas equation estimates PAO₂ using PaCO₂ and respiratory quotient. The alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient depends on age, inspired oxygen and measurement conditions.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Physiological mechanism

At 37 °C inspired gas is humidified to water-vapor pressure 47 mmHg. Therefore PIO₂=(PB−47)·FiO₂. The simplified alveolar gas equation PAO₂≈PIO₂−PaCO₂/R assumes near-steady state and depends on its assumptions and respiratory quotient R.

Worked physiological example

At sea level with barometric pressure 760 mmHg, humidified inspired oxygen has PIO₂≈(760−47)×0.21≈150 mmHg at body temperature.

Gas composition and partial pressures

Examination: eight questions

1. At PB = 760 mmHg and FIO₂ = 0.21, approximate PIO₂ at 37 °C?

0.21 × (760 − 47) ≈ 150. The 159 figure is for dry air.

2. For PB = 760, FIO₂ = 0.21, PaCO₂ = 40 and R = 0.8, estimate PAO₂.

PAO₂ ≈ 0.21(760 − 47) − 40/0.8 ≈ 100 mmHg.

PIO₂ depends on PB: FIO₂(PB − 47).

A–a = 100 − 65 = 35 mmHg.

PaCO₂ varies inversely with V̇A at constant V̇CO₂.

With isolated hypoventilation, PAO₂ and PaO₂ fall together; A–a is often near normal.

PaO₂ is the partial pressure of dissolved O₂; CaO₂ includes hemoglobin-bound and dissolved O₂.

R = V̇CO₂/V̇O₂; around 0.8 in steady state on a mixed diet.

11/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Physiological mechanisms

1. The blood–air barrier

Oxygen crosses the surfactant-lined fluid layer, alveolar epithelium, basement membranes, interstitium and capillary endothelium. In thin regions the basement membranes are closely apposed; thicker regions offer a longer diffusion path. Oxygen then crosses plasma and the erythrocyte membrane before binding haemoglobin. Gas exchange therefore depends on area, thickness, capillary transit time and red-cell properties.

2. Fick’s diffusion law

In a simplified model gas flux is proportional to surface area A, diffusion coefficient D and partial-pressure difference ΔP, and inversely proportional to barrier thickness T: V̇gas = (D·A/T)·ΔP. Doubling thickness halves flux when all other factors are held constant. In real lungs capillary recruitment, area and the gradient along each capillary vary together; this model illustrates direction rather than predicting arterial PO₂.

3. O₂ versus CO₂

CO₂ is much more soluble in tissue fluids than O₂ and therefore has a greater diffusing capacity despite a smaller partial-pressure gradient. Severe pulmonary disease can nevertheless impair CO₂ removal, particularly when ventilation falls. The pressure gradient alone does not determine gas transfer.

4. Capillary transit time

At rest capillary transit is approximately 0.75 s, while blood PO₂ normally approaches alveolar PO₂ during the earlier part of transit. Exercise shortens transit time but capillary recruitment and distension preserve diffusion reserve in healthy lungs. Thickening of the barrier or low alveolar PO₂ reduces that reserve and can reveal exertional hypoxaemia.

5. Perfusion and diffusion limitation

A perfusion-limited gas equilibrates early along the capillary, so additional transfer mainly depends on blood flow. A diffusion-limited gas does not equilibrate by the capillary end. Oxygen transfer is usually perfusion-limited at rest in healthy lungs; fibrosis, intense exercise or high-altitude hypoxia may introduce diffusion limitation. Carbon monoxide is used to assess diffusing capacity because its capillary partial pressure remains very low.

6. What DLCO measures

DLCO estimates uptake of a small amount of CO from alveolar gas into blood per unit time and pressure difference. It depends on membrane properties, capillary blood volume, haemoglobin and alveolar volume. Anaemia can reduce measured DLCO without barrier thickening; polycythaemia or alveolar haemorrhage may raise it. Interpretation requires haemoglobin adjustment, manoeuvre quality and appropriate reference equations, not one universal cutoff.

7. A–a difference and hypoxaemia

An increased alveolar–arterial O₂ difference indicates impaired transfer from alveolar gas to arterial blood but is not specific for a diffusion defect: V/Q mismatch and shunt are common causes. In isolated hypoventilation the A–a difference is generally age-appropriate. Compare measured PaO₂ with estimated PAO₂ using FiO₂, barometric pressure, PaCO₂ and respiratory quotient.

8. Fibrosis, emphysema and oedema

Interstitial fibrosis increases effective diffusion distance and may reduce available surface; emphysema destroys alveolar septa and capillary bed; oedema lengthens the pathway and often causes V/Q heterogeneity. Reduced DLCO is therefore not attributable to a single mechanism without other data. Interpret it alongside spirometry, lung volumes, haemoglobin, imaging and blood gases.

Academic foundation

The blood–air barrier includes alveolar epithelium, basement membranes, interstitium and capillary endothelium. Oxygen transfer can be diffusion- or perfusion-limited depending on conditions and red-cell transit time. DLCO reflects membrane conductance together with accessible pulmonary capillary blood volume.

11/questions/EN.html:
Discussion

Teaching draft

Discussion questions

  • Why is DLCO not simply membrane thickness?
  • How can diffusion limitation and V/Q mismatch be distinguished?
  • How does diffusion reserve change during exercise?
  • Why is CO₂ usually less sensitive to moderate barrier thickening?

Diffusion and perfusion limitation

Fick’s law describes gas flux across a barrier: V̇gas ∝ A × D × ΔP/T. Here A is exchange area, T membrane thickness, D a diffusion coefficient and ΔP the partial-pressure gradient. Interstitial thickening reduces flux all else equal, but actual oxygenation also depends on blood flow and erythrocyte transit time.

In healthy lungs oxygen usually equilibrates with alveolar gas before capillary exit, so uptake is predominantly perfusion-limited. Interstitial disease, exercise or altitude can reduce diffusion reserve and reveal diffusion limitation. CO₂ has a higher effective diffusing capacity, although severe abnormalities can impair transfer of both gases.

Physiology reasoning task

At fixed A, D and ΔP, membrane thickness doubles. How does flux change in the simplified Fick model? Why does this not predict PaO₂ exactly?

Show solution

Flux halves; PaO₂ also depends on V/Q, perfusion, hemoglobin and transit time.

Discussion with explanation

Why does reduced DLCO not prove interstitial fibrosis?

Show explanation

DLCO depends on membrane transfer, capillary blood volume, hemoglobin and maneuver quality. Anemia, emphysema and vascular disease can also lower it; diagnosis requires additional evidence.

12/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Pulmonary circulation: flow, pressure, vascular tone and gas exchange

1. Two vascular circuits

The pulmonary circuit carries the entire right-ventricular cardiac output through pulmonary capillaries. Systemic bronchial arteries nourish conducting airways; some bronchial venous blood drains to pulmonary veins, contributing to normal venous admixture. These are distinct circuits.

2. Pressure and resistance

At rest mean pulmonary artery pressure is often near 14–15 mmHg and wedge pressure near 6–12 mmHg, depending on measurement conditions. Pulmonary vascular resistance PVR = (mPAP − PAWP)/CO, expressed in Wood units (mmHg·min/L). With 15, 8 and 5 L/min, PVR is 1.4 WU. These example values are not diagnostic thresholds.

3. Recruitment and distension

As cardiac output rises, previously underperfused capillaries recruit and open capillaries distend. Flow can therefore rise markedly during exercise with a smaller rise in mean pressure; the pressure–flow relationship is not strictly linear.

4. Gravity and West zones

Upright posture creates a hydrostatic vascular-pressure gradient. West zones describe relations between alveolar PA, arterial Pa and venous Pv pressure: zone 1 PA > Pa > Pv; zone 2 Pa > PA > Pv; zone 3 Pa > Pv > PA. These are idealized physiological states, not fixed anatomical layers.

5. Alveolar and extra-alveolar vessels

At high lung volume, stretched alveolar walls compress alveolar capillaries, whereas radial traction expands extra-alveolar vessels. The combined resistance often follows a U-shaped relation to lung volume, with a minimum around functional residual capacity.

6. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction

Low alveolar PO₂ locally constricts small pulmonary arteries and diverts blood from poorly ventilated units. This contrasts with typical systemic arteriolar dilation in tissue hypoxia. Widespread hypoxia can increase total PVR and right-ventricular afterload.

7. Endothelium and mediators

Endothelial nitric oxide and prostacyclin favor dilation; endothelin-1 promotes constriction and remodeling. Vascular tone reflects mechanical forces, oxygen availability, endothelial signaling and smooth muscle responses rather than one mediator alone.

8. Edema and lymph drainage

Fluid movement depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces, endothelial permeability and lymphatic drainage. Elevated pulmonary venous pressure promotes filtration, whereas barrier injury raises permeability. Alveolar edema lengthens diffusion paths and worsens V/Q matching.

9. Right ventricular afterload

The right ventricle is adapted to a low-resistance circuit. Higher PVR increases afterload, may reduce stroke volume and can cause right-ventricular dilation. Pressure alone cannot define resistance without flow and downstream filling pressure.

10. Clinical interpretation

Right-heart catheterization interprets mPAP, PAWP and CO together. Hypoxemia does not necessarily imply elevated PVR; pulmonary hypertension requires distinction between increased pulmonary resistance and increased left-sided filling pressure. Teaching calculations do not replace clinical assessment.

Academic foundation

Pulmonary vessels operate at low pressure and relatively low resistance. Increased cardiac output generally recruits and distends capillaries. Local alveolar hypoxia causes vasoconstriction that redistributes flow, whereas widespread hypoxia can raise pulmonary vascular resistance.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Physiological mechanism

Conceptual checkpoint

Pulmonary vascular resistance varies with flow and vascular recruitment; it is not a fixed constant.

Worked physiological example

Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction diverts flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli; widespread hypoxia may increase pulmonary vascular resistance.

Conditions and limitations

12/glossary/EN.html:
Glossary

Teaching draft

Pulmonary circulation: flow, pressure, vascular tone and gas exchange

Two vascular circuits
The pulmonary circuit carries the entire right-ventricular cardiac output through pulmonary capillaries.
Pressure and resistance
At rest mean pulmonary artery pressure is often near 14–15 mmHg and wedge pressure near 6–12 mmHg, depending on measurement conditions.
Recruitment and distension
As cardiac output rises, previously underperfused capillaries recruit and open capillaries distend.
Gravity and West zones
Upright posture creates a hydrostatic vascular-pressure gradient.
Alveolar and extra-alveolar vessels
At high lung volume, stretched alveolar walls compress alveolar capillaries, whereas radial traction expands extra-alveolar vessels.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
Low alveolar PO₂ locally constricts small pulmonary arteries and diverts blood from poorly ventilated units.
Endothelium and mediators
Endothelial nitric oxide and prostacyclin favor dilation; endothelin-1 promotes constriction and remodeling.
Edema and lymph drainage
Fluid movement depends on hydrostatic and oncotic forces, endothelial permeability and lymphatic drainage.
Right ventricular afterload
The right ventricle is adapted to a low-resistance circuit.
Clinical interpretation
Right-heart catheterization interprets mPAP, PAWP and CO together.

13/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Ventilation–perfusion relationships

1. Definition of V/Q

The V/Q ratio is alveolar ventilation divided by pulmonary blood flow. Whole-lung values of 4.2 and 5 L/min give approximately 0.84. This is a ratio of total flows, not the arithmetic mean of local ratios.

2. Regional heterogeneity

In upright lungs, both ventilation and perfusion usually increase toward the bases, but perfusion increases more steeply. V/Q is consequently higher at the apex than at the base. Posture, gravity, vascular geometry and lung volume all matter.

3. Alveolar gas composition

At high V/Q, alveolar PO₂ approaches humidified inspired PO₂ and PCO₂ falls. At low V/Q, alveolar gas approaches mixed venous values: PO₂ decreases and PCO₂ rises. Actual values depend on gas exchange and regional flow.

4. Low V/Q

Poorly ventilated yet perfused units contribute blood with reduced oxygen content. Low V/Q is a common cause of an increased alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient. Supplemental oxygen generally improves oxygenation when ventilation is reduced but not absent.

5. High V/Q

When perfusion is low relative to ventilation, some ventilation is wasted because little blood is available for gas exchange. Markedly underperfused units approach alveolar dead space.

6. Shunt: V/Q = 0

Blood crossing a perfused but unventilated unit cannot equilibrate with fresh alveolar gas. This is intrapulmonary shunt, as in a fully fluid-filled or collapsed unit. True shunt responds much less to increased FiO₂ than low nonzero V/Q.

7. Dead space: V/Q → ∞

With ventilation but zero perfusion, V/Q is formally undefined (conventionally tends toward infinity), and exchange with blood ceases. This idealized alveolar dead-space condition may occur downstream of an occluded pulmonary artery.

8. Why high V/Q cannot fully compensate

Blood oxygen content rises nonlinearly with PO₂ owing to the sigmoid hemoglobin saturation curve. Well-ventilated units are already near full saturation, so their extra PO₂ adds little oxygen content and cannot fully offset low-V/Q blood.

9. Hypoxic vasoconstriction

Local alveolar hypoxia constricts small pulmonary arteries, redirecting flow toward better ventilated units. It cannot completely abolish severe shunt, and diffuse hypoxia can increase pulmonary vascular resistance.

10. Alveolar–arterial O₂ gradient

Under steady conditions PAO₂ ≈ FiO₂(PB−PH₂O)−PaCO₂/R, and the A–a gradient is PAO₂−PaO₂. On room air at sea level with 0.21, 760, 47, 40 mmHg and R 0.8, PAO₂ is about 100 mmHg. The gradient varies with age and FiO₂.

11. Effect of posture

Supine positioning redistributes ventilation and perfusion along a different gravitational axis. In unilateral lung disease, posture may affect oxygenation, but the effect depends on the disorder and respiratory mechanics.

12. Exercise and recruitment

During exercise, cardiac output and alveolar ventilation rise; capillary recruitment and distension can improve perfusion distribution. Heavy exertion, age and disease can alter exchange efficiency.

13. Pulmonary embolism and high V/Q

Pulmonary arterial occlusion reduces flow while ventilation persists, increasing alveolar dead space. Hypoxemia in pulmonary embolism may additionally reflect redistributed flow, low-V/Q regions and other mechanisms; high V/Q alone is not the full explanation.

14. Atelectasis and shunt

A collapsed but perfused alveolar unit has V/Q near zero. Venous admixture lowers arterial oxygenation; severity depends on shunt fraction. Clinical assessment requires more than a single SpO₂ value.

15. Limitations of simplified models

Real lungs contain many units spanning a continuum of V/Q. Mixed blood oxygen is determined by oxygen content, not arithmetic averaging of PO₂. Quantitative assessment requires flows, hemoglobin, blood gases and sometimes multicompartment models.

Academic foundation

V/Q describes matching of alveolar ventilation to blood flow. V/Q near zero creates shunt-like behaviour, whereas very high V/Q wastes ventilation. Mixed blood streams must be combined by oxygen content rather than PaO₂ because haemoglobin oxygen binding is nonlinear.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Shunt and blood mixing

A true shunt allows venous blood to enter systemic circulation without contact with ventilated alveoli. Oxygen contents, not PO₂ values, are mixed; averaging partial pressures is physiologically incorrect.

Student exercise: Given Cc′O₂ = 20 mL/dL, CvO₂ = 15 mL/dL and shunt fraction 0.20, calculate CaO₂. Explain why PaO₂ cannot be inferred by linear interpolation.

Worked solution

CaO₂ = 0.80 × 20 + 0.20 × 15 = 19 mL/dL. Oxygen content and PO₂ are nonlinearly related through hemoglobin dissociation; further assumptions are needed to infer PaO₂.

Physiological mechanism

The V̇A/Q̇ ratio describes matching of alveolar ventilation to perfusion. As V/Q approaches zero, blood traverses poorly ventilated units, producing a shunt-like effect; as V/Q approaches infinity, ventilation reaches poorly perfused units and contributes to alveolar dead space. These limits are not identical to an anatomical shunt. When blood streams mix, oxygen contents—not PO₂ values—are averaged.

Reference reading: West, Respiratory Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology; ERS/ATS (spirometry).

Conceptual checkpoint

When blood streams mix, average O₂ content rather than PaO₂ because hemoglobin binding is nonlinear.

Worked physiological example

Shunt means perfusion without effective ventilation; alveolar dead space means ventilation without adequate perfusion.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

Two equal blood flows mix, with O₂ contents of 20 and 16 mL/dL. Find mixed O₂ content. Can averaging their PO₂ values instead reliably predict arterial PO₂?

Worked solution

Cmixed=(Q₁C₁+Q₂C₂)/(Q₁+Q₂)=(20+16)/2=18 mL/dL. Unequal flows require flow-weighted mixing rather than a simple arithmetic mean.

Meaning and model limitations

Mixing conserves O₂ amount. Content relates nonlinearly to PO₂ through hemoglobin, so pressures cannot simply be averaged. High V/Q cannot fully compensate low V/Q because extra PO₂ adds little content on the Hb plateau.

14/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Transport of oxygen in blood

1. Forms of oxygen carriage

Most oxygen is reversibly bound to red-cell hemoglobin; a small fraction is dissolved in plasma. Dissolved oxygen determines PaO₂ and the diffusion gradient, whereas hemoglobin supplies most oxygen-carrying capacity. Increasing dissolved oxygen at ordinary pressures cannot replace a major loss of hemoglobin.

2. Arterial oxygen content

With Hb in g/dL, SaO₂ as a fraction and PaO₂ in mmHg, arterial oxygen content CaO₂ (mL O₂/dL blood) ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.0031 × PaO₂. These coefficients are approximations. With Hb 15, saturation 0.98 and PaO₂ 100, CaO₂ ≈ 20.01 mL/dL; just 0.31 mL/dL is dissolved.

3. Hemoglobin and cooperativity

Adult HbA contains two alpha and two beta chains, each with a heme capable of binding one O₂ molecule. Binding facilitates subsequent binding on other subunits, producing a sigmoid saturation curve. Cooperativity supports loading in the lungs and unloading in tissues.

4. Oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve

The upper plateau preserves saturation despite moderate falls in alveolar PO₂, while the steep portion supports tissue unloading. Under standard conditions, SaO₂ is near 97–99% at PaO₂ around 100 mmHg and saturation is roughly 75% at PO₂ around 40 mmHg; pH, temperature and 2,3-BPG affect these values.

5. P50 and hemoglobin affinity

P50 is the PO₂ at 50% hemoglobin saturation. For adult HbA under standard conditions it is about 26–27 mmHg. Increased P50 indicates reduced affinity (right shift), and decreased P50 increased affinity (left shift). P50 does not directly measure tissue oxygen delivery.

6. Bohr effect

Increased PCO₂ and H⁺ (lower pH) decrease Hb affinity for O₂ and shift the curve right, aiding unloading in metabolically active tissue. Lower PCO₂ in the lungs supports O₂ binding. The Bohr effect differs from the Haldane effect.

7. Temperature and 2,3-BPG

Higher temperature and erythrocyte 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate generally shift the curve right. 2,3-BPG stabilizes deoxygenated hemoglobin. Levels may rise during chronic hypoxia, depending on red-cell state and adaptation time.

8. Fetal Hb, CO and methemoglobin

Fetal HbF has higher O₂ affinity than HbA partly due to reduced interaction with 2,3-BPG. Carbon monoxide occupies heme sites and shifts remaining binding toward higher affinity. Methemoglobin contains Fe³⁺ and cannot bind O₂ normally. Conventional pulse oximetry may be misleading with dyshemoglobins.

9. Oxygen delivery and consumption

Oxygen delivery DO₂ (mL/min) = cardiac output (L/min) × CaO₂ (mL/dL) × 10. At 5 L/min and 20 mL/dL, DO₂ is about 1000 mL/min. By Fick, VO₂ = cardiac output × (CaO₂ − CvO₂) × 10. Resting VO₂ is often around 250 mL/min but varies with body size and metabolism.

10. Anemia versus hypoxemia

Anemia can leave PaO₂ and SaO₂ normal while lowering CaO₂ and DO₂ because Hb concentration is reduced. Hypoxemia lowers PaO₂ and often saturation and oxygen content. SpO₂ alone cannot establish oxygen delivery: Hb, flow and context matter.

11. Tissue oxygen extraction

O₂ extraction ratio = VO₂/DO₂ = (CaO₂−CvO₂)/CaO₂ in a simple steady-state model. When delivery falls, tissues may increase extraction until a critical limit. Local perfusion, microcirculation and mitochondrial function also matter.

12. Measuring SaO₂, SpO₂ and PaO₂

PaO₂ is measured in arterial blood gas analysis; SaO₂ may be measured by co-oximetry or estimated from gases; SpO₂ is estimated optically. SpO₂ does not measure Hb, CaO₂ or DO₂. Standard two-wavelength oximeters may appear normal in CO poisoning.

Academic foundation

Most oxygen is carried by haemoglobin, with a small dissolved fraction. PaO₂, SaO₂ and CaO₂ measure different aspects of oxygen transport. Oxygen delivery depends on CaO₂ and cardiac output; normal saturation does not exclude inadequate delivery in anaemia.

Subsection task

Analyse the causal chain: initial condition → physical or cellular process → change in a measurable variable → functional consequence.

Methodological limitation: Physiological values depend on age, measurement conditions and patient state. Schematic models are not individual clinical predictions.

Saturation versus oxygen content

Pulse oximetry estimates the fraction of oxygenated hemoglobin, not hemoglobin concentration. In anemia SpO₂ can be normal despite reduced CaO₂ and oxygen delivery.

Student exercise: Compare CaO₂ at Hb 15 and 8 g/dL with SaO₂ 98% and PaO₂ 95 mmHg. Use CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂.

Worked solution

At Hb 15: ≈19.98 mL/dL; at Hb 8: ≈10.79 mL/dL. Oxygen content falls markedly despite identical saturation.

Physiological mechanism

Arterial oxygen content depends mainly on haemoglobin: CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂, with Hb in g/dL, SaO₂ as a fraction, PaO₂ in mmHg, and CaO₂ in mL O₂/dL. PaO₂ reflects dissolved-gas pressure, SaO₂ the fraction of occupied haemoglobin sites, and CaO₂ total oxygen content. Anaemia can reduce CaO₂ despite normal PaO₂ and SaO₂.

Reference reading: West, Respiratory Physiology; Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology; ERS/ATS (spirometry).

Conceptual checkpoint

SaO₂, PaO₂ and CaO₂ are distinct quantities; anemia may preserve saturation despite low O₂ content.

Worked physiological example

At Hb 15 g/dL and SaO₂ 98%, hemoglobin-bound O₂ ≈1.34×15×0.98≈19.7 mL/dL; dissolved O₂ is much smaller.

Conditions and limitations

The example illustrates a mechanism; numerical values depend on conditions and are not individual reference limits.

Practice

Teaching draft

Transport of oxygen in blood

  1. Hb 12 g/dL, SaO₂ 0.95, PaO₂ 80: calculate CaO₂ and both component contributions.
  2. Compare DO₂ at Hb 8 versus 16 g/dL with SaO₂ 0.98, PaO₂ 100 and output 5 L/min.

Calculation and physiological interpretation

Hb=10 g/dL, SaO₂=98% and PaO₂=100 mmHg. Find CaO₂ with Hb capacity 1.34 mL O₂/g and solubility coefficient 0.003 mL O₂/(dL·mmHg). Then halve Hb at unchanged SaO₂ and PaO₂.

CaO₂=1.34×10×0.98+0.003×100=13.432 mL/dL. At Hb=5, CaO₂=6.866 mL/dL. Bound O₂ halves while dissolved O₂ remains 0.30 mL/dL.

PaO₂ describes dissolved-gas pressure, SaO₂ the occupied fraction of available Hb sites, and CaO₂ the O₂ amount per blood volume. Normal pressure and saturation do not exclude reduced content in anemia. Dyshemoglobins need separate assessment.

1. With Hb 10 g/dL, SaO₂ 0.98 and PaO₂ 100 mmHg, approximate CaO₂?

15/theory/EN.html:
Theory

Teaching draft

Carbon dioxide transport in blood

1. Tissue CO₂ production

CO₂ arises from oxidative metabolism. Resting V̇CO₂ is often about 200 mL/min but varies with body size, substrate and metabolism. It diffuses from tissues into capillaries along a partial-pressure gradient.

2. Three transport forms

CO₂ travels dissolved, as bicarbonate, and as carbamino compounds, notably on hemoglobin. Approximate textbook shares are 5–10%, 60–70%, and 20–30%, respectively; they vary with conditions and definitions and are not universal constants.

3. Dissolved CO₂ and Henry’s law

Dissolved CO₂ is proportional to PCO₂. At 37 °C, plasma solubility is approximately 0.03 mmol/(L·mmHg); at 40 mmHg dissolved CO₂ is about 1.2 mmol/L. This is not total blood CO₂ content.

4. Carbonic anhydrase

Erythrocyte carbonic anhydrase accelerates reversible CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. Bicarbonate formation predominates during tissue uptake; in the lungs the reaction shifts toward CO₂ release.

5. Hemoglobin buffering

Deoxygenated hemoglobin binds many of the protons produced by CO₂ hydration, buffering intracellular pH and favoring bicarbonate formation. Hemoglobin buffering depends on oxygenation.

6. Chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon)

In tissue capillaries, bicarbonate exits red cells in exchange for chloride through AE1 (band 3), preserving electroneutrality and permitting plasma bicarbonate transport. The exchange reverses in pulmonary capillaries.

7. Carbamino compounds

CO₂ binds reversibly to terminal amino groups of proteins, particularly globin chains, forming carbaminohemoglobin. This is distinct from carboxyhemoglobin formed by carbon monoxide binding to heme. Deoxygenation favors carbamino binding.

8. Haldane effect

At the same PCO₂, deoxygenated blood carries more total CO₂ than oxygenated blood because deoxyhemoglobin buffers H⁺ and binds CO₂ more readily. Oxygenation in the lungs aids CO₂ unloading. Haldane concerns O₂ effects on CO₂ transport; Bohr concerns CO₂/H⁺ effects on Hb–O₂ affinity.

9. CO₂ content curve

Total CO₂ content increases with PCO₂ and depends on Hb oxygen saturation. At a given PCO₂, the deoxygenated blood content curve lies above the oxygenated curve. It is not a universal linear formula.

10. Venoarterial CO₂ difference

Mixed venous PCO₂ is usually higher than arterial PCO₂ (roughly 46 versus 40 mmHg at rest). Pressure differences are not content differences. Fick’s principle gives V̇CO₂ = Q̇ × (CvCO₂ − CaCO₂) using consistent content units.

11. Alveolar ventilation and PaCO₂

At steady state PaCO₂ ≈ 0.863 × V̇CO₂ / V̇A, with CO₂ output in mL/min STPD and alveolar ventilation in L/min BTPS. At 200 mL/min and 4.3 L/min, PaCO₂ is about 40 mmHg. Rapid transitions and marked V/Q mismatch complicate this approximation.

12. Henderson–Hasselbalch equation

For the extracellular bicarbonate buffer at 37 °C, pH ≈ 6.1 + log₁₀([HCO₃⁻]/(0.03 × PaCO₂)); bicarbonate is in mmol/L and PaCO₂ in mmHg. Values 24 and 40 give pH ≈ 7.40. This relation alone does not identify the underlying disorder.

13. Hypoventilation and hypercapnia

At constant CO₂ production, lower alveolar ventilation raises PaCO₂ and tends to lower pH. Causes include reduced respiratory drive, muscle weakness and severe obstruction. High total minute ventilation does not exclude hypercapnia if dead space is large.

14. Hyperventilation and hypocapnia

When CO₂ production is approximately constant, increased alveolar ventilation reduces PaCO₂ and favors respiratory alkalosis. Hyperventilation is defined relative to metabolic CO₂ production, not by respiratory rate alone.

15. Limits of blood gas interpretation

PaCO₂ reflects CO₂ production relative to effective alveolar ventilation. Interpret alongside pH, bicarbonate, PaO₂, FiO₂, clinical context and time course. Venous measurements are not interchangeable with arterial reference ranges.

Academic foundation

CO₂ is transported dissolved, as bicarbonate and as carbamino compounds. Red-cell carbonic anhydrase accelerates CO₂ hydration, and AE1 mediates chloride shift. The Haldane effect describes greater CO₂ carriage and H⁺ buffering by deoxygenated haemoglobin, other conditions equal.
